summary.overview: Vitamins are essential dietary factors needed in small amounts, mainly as coenzymes or hormone precursors. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed with fat and stored; water-soluble vitamins (B complex, C) are mostly not stored (B12 is the exception). Species differ a lot in what they must eat, which matters greatly in veterinary practice.

sections.heading: Vitamin A
points: Retinoids: retinol (alcohol), retinal (aldehyde) and retinoic acid (acid). β-Carotene from plants is a provitamin, cleaved by a dioxygenase in the gut. Cats cannot do this efficiently and need preformed vitamin A.
Absorbed with fat (needs bile salts), carried in chylomicrons, stored in liver stellate cells as retinyl palmitate, and carried to tissues by retinol-binding protein.
Vision (Wald's cycle): 11-cis-retinal + opsin = rhodopsin. Light isomerises it to all-trans, activating a G protein. Deficiency causes night blindness.
Retinoic acid acts like a steroid hormone on nuclear receptors (gene expression, epithelia, reproduction). Its RXR receptor partners with the vitamin D receptor.
Deficiency in livestock: poor growth, night blindness, infections, abortion, weak calves. Excess (hypervitaminosis A): liver enlargement, skin peeling, anorexia.

sections.heading: Vitamin D
points: D3 (cholecalciferol) forms from 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin exposed to UV; D2 (ergocalciferol) comes from ergosterol in fungi and plants. Dogs and cats make very little in their skin, so they rely on their diet.
It is hydroxylated in the liver (25-OH) and then the kidney (1α-OH) to calcitriol, the active hormone.
Calcitriol binds a receptor that acts as a transcription factor, inducing calbindin. This increases intestinal Ca²⁺ and phosphate absorption and renal reabsorption, and supports bone mineralisation.
Deficiency causes rickets and bone disease. Excess causes hypercalcaemia and soft-tissue calcification, e.g. cholecalciferol rodenticide poisoning in dogs.

sections.heading: Vitamins E and K
points: Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) is the main lipid-soluble antioxidant: it breaks lipid-peroxidation chains in membranes and protects red cells.
E deficiency (often with low selenium, or poor hay) causes white muscle disease (nutritional muscular dystrophy) in calves and lambs, mulberry heart disease in pigs, and crazy chick disease.
Vitamin K: K1 from plants, K2 from gut bacteria, K3 (menadione) synthetic. It is the cofactor for γ-carboxylation of Glu in clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and in osteocalcin.
Warfarin, anticoagulant rodenticides and dicoumarol (from mouldy sweet clover) block vitamin K recycling, causing bleeding; vitamin K1 is the antidote.

sections.heading: B-complex vitamins → coenzymes
points: B1 thiamine → TPP: pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase. Deficiency raises pyruvate and lactate (beriberi; polioencephalomalacia in ruminants).
B2 riboflavin → FMN, FAD. B3 niacin → NAD⁺, NADP⁺; niacin can be made from Trp (not efficiently in cats); deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia).
B5 pantothenic acid → coenzyme A and acyl carrier protein. B6 pyridoxine → PLP for transamination, amino acid decarboxylation, ALA synthase and glycogen phosphorylase.
B7 biotin → carboxylases (acetyl-CoA carboxylase, pyruvate carboxylase); avidin in raw egg white binds it.
B9 folate → tetrahydrofolate, a one-carbon carrier needed for thymidylate and DNA synthesis. Deficiency → megaloblastic (macrocytic) anaemia.

B12 cobalamin (contains cobalt): methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase. Absorption needs intrinsic factor. Deficiency causes the 'methyl-folate trap' (secondary folate deficiency), megaloblastic anaemia, raised homocysteine and demyelination. Ruminal microbes make B12 only if there is enough cobalt in the diet.

sections.heading: Vitamin C
points: L-Ascorbic acid is a strong reducing agent. Most animals make it from glucose; primates, guinea pigs and fruit bats cannot.
Roles: hydroxylation of Pro and Lys in collagen, iron absorption (keeps iron as Fe²⁺), reducing methaemoglobin, folate reduction, and antioxidant defence.
Deficiency causes scurvy: fragile capillaries, bleeding gums, poor coat, painful joints, anaemia. It is easily destroyed by heat and storage.

keyTerms.definition: Precursor converted into an active vitamin, e.g. β-carotene → retinal.
1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, the active hormone form of vitamin D.
Vitamin K-dependent addition of CO2 to Glu residues of clotting factors.
Thiamine pyrophosphate, coenzyme for oxidative decarboxylation and transketolase.
Pyridoxal phosphate (B6), coenzyme for transamination and decarboxylation.
Gastric protein required for vitamin B12 absorption.
Folate locked as methyl-THF when B12 is lacking, causing functional folate deficiency.

examTips: Fat-soluble = A, D, E, K: absorbed with fat (bile salts), stored, so toxicity is possible.
Match each B vitamin to its coenzyme: B1 TPP, B2 FAD/FMN, B3 NAD(P), B5 CoA, B6 PLP, B7 biotin, B9 THF, B12 cobalamin.
Vitamin K: clotting factors II, VII, IX, X; warfarin and rodenticides block it.
Species quirks: cats need preformed vitamin A, extra niacin and dietary vitamin D; guinea pigs need vitamin C; ruminants need cobalt to make B12.

questions.stem: Which group lists only fat-soluble vitamins?

options.text: A, D, E and K
options.why: They are absorbed with dietary fat (needing bile salts) and can be stored, so excess intake can be toxic.

options.text: B1, B2, B6 and B12
options.why: These are water-soluble B-complex vitamins.

options.text: A, C, D and B12
options.why: C and B12 are water-soluble.

options.text: C, E, K and biotin
options.why: C and biotin are water-soluble.

questions.stem: A home-made vegan diet for a cat relies on carrots as its vitamin A source. Why is this inadequate?

options.text: Cats cannot efficiently cleave β-carotene into retinal, so they need preformed vitamin A
options.why: β-Carotene is only a provitamin; cats lack enough of the converting dioxygenase activity.

options.text: Carrots contain no β-carotene; their orange colour comes from lycopene, which has no vitamin A activity
options.why: Carrots are rich in β-carotene.

options.text: Vitamin A is water-soluble and is lost into the cooking water when the carrots are boiled
options.why: Vitamin A is fat-soluble.

options.text: Cats make their vitamin A in their skin under sunlight, so dietary sources are not used
options.why: Skin synthesis applies to vitamin D (and cats do even that poorly).

questions.stem: Why does vitamin A deficiency cause night blindness?

options.text: Rods need 11-cis-retinal to regenerate rhodopsin after light isomerises it, so dark adaptation fails
options.why: Rhodopsin = opsin + 11-cis-retinal; bright light bleaches it.

options.text: Retinoic acid is the light-absorbing molecule of the cone cells only, so dim-light vision is lost first
options.why: The visual chromophore is 11-cis-retinal in rods and cones.

options.text: Vitamin A is needed to keep the lens transparent, and a cloudy lens blocks most of the light at night
options.why: The defect is in pigment regeneration in the retina.

options.text: Vitamin A deficiency stops calcium absorption, and the retina's rods need calcium to send signals
options.why: That is vitamin D's role.

questions.stem: How does retinoic acid regulate tissue differentiation?

options.text: Like a steroid hormone, it binds nuclear receptors that act as transcription factors
options.why: 9-cis-retinoic acid binds RXR, which also partners with the vitamin D receptor.

options.text: It acts as a coenzyme for transaminases, which supply the amino acids that new cells need
options.why: That is PLP (vitamin B6).

options.text: It carboxylates clotting factors and growth proteins, so they can bind calcium in tissues
options.why: That is vitamin K.

options.text: It is the visual chromophore in rhodopsin, which signals cells to divide when light hits it
options.why: The chromophore is 11-cis-retinal, not retinoic acid.

questions.stem: Vitamin D3 is biologically inactive until it is converted to calcitriol. Where do the two activating hydroxylations occur?

options.text: At C-25 in the liver, then at C-1 in the kidney
options.why: 25-hydroxylation then 1α-hydroxylation give 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol).

options.text: Both in the skin, driven directly by UV light
options.why: UV makes previtamin D3 from 7-dehydrocholesterol; hydroxylation is enzymatic in liver and kidney.

options.text: First in the intestine, then in the bone
options.why: These are target tissues, not activation sites.

options.text: In the red blood cells and the spleen
options.why: Red cells are not involved.

questions.stem: How does calcitriol increase intestinal calcium absorption?

options.text: It binds its receptor, which acts on DNA to switch on genes such as calbindin (Ca²⁺-binding)
options.why: Calcitriol acts like a steroid hormone, increasing transcription of Ca²⁺-transport proteins.

options.text: It inserts directly into the gut membrane, forming channels through which the calcium ions flow
options.why: It acts through gene expression.

options.text: It is a coenzyme for calcium kinase, which phosphorylates calcium so that it can be absorbed
options.why: There is no such coenzyme role.

options.text: It inhibits alkaline phosphatase in the gut wall, so less calcium is lost as calcium phosphate
options.why: It stimulates alkaline phosphatase, aiding mineralisation.

questions.stem: A dog has eaten a cholecalciferol-based rodenticide. What is the main biochemical danger?

options.text: Hypercalcaemia from excess vitamin D activity, calcifying soft tissues such as the kidneys
options.why: Hypervitaminosis D increases Ca²⁺ absorption and mobilisation, mineralising soft tissue and causing kidney failure.

options.text: Bleeding, because clotting factors are no longer carboxylated, so the blood cannot clot
options.why: That is the effect of anticoagulant (vitamin K antagonist) rodenticides.

options.text: Night blindness, because the rods can no longer regenerate their rhodopsin
options.why: That is a vitamin A deficiency sign.

options.text: Scurvy, because the excess vitamin D blocks the hydroxylation of collagen
options.why: Scurvy is vitamin C deficiency.

questions.stem: Young lambs on poor-quality hay and selenium-deficient pasture develop stiffness, difficulty rising and pale streaks in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely, and why does it damage muscle?

options.text: Vitamin E: without this membrane antioxidant, lipid peroxidation damages muscle (white muscle disease)
options.why: Vitamin E and selenium (glutathione peroxidase) together protect membranes from oxidative damage.

options.text: Vitamin K: without it clotting factors are inactive, so the muscles bleed internally and become pale
options.why: Vitamin K deficiency mainly causes coagulation defects.

options.text: Vitamin D: without it calcium is not absorbed, so the muscles calcify and become stiff and streaked
options.why: Calcification is a sign of vitamin D excess.

options.text: Vitamin B12: without it muscle cannot make methionine, so its fibres cannot build contractile proteins
options.why: This is not the mechanism of nutritional myopathy.

questions.stem: What is the biochemical role of vitamin K in blood clotting?

options.text: It is the cofactor for γ-carboxylating Glu residues in factors II, VII, IX and X, so they bind Ca²⁺
options.why: Without γ-carboxyglutamate, these factors cannot work.

options.text: It hydroxylates proline residues in fibrinogen, which lets the fibrin strands cross-link into a clot
options.why: Prolyl hydroxylation (collagen) needs vitamin C.

options.text: It is the coenzyme for transamination of the clotting factors, which activates them in the plasma
options.why: That is PLP (B6).

options.text: It directly forms the fibrin clot by polymerising at the site of injury, together with platelets
options.why: Fibrin is a protein; vitamin K modifies the clotting factors.

questions.stem: A dog has prolonged clotting times and bruising after eating an anticoagulant rodenticide. What is the mechanism, and the antidote?

options.text: It blocks vitamin K recycling (epoxide reductase), so new clotting factors aren't carboxylated; give K1
options.why: Warfarin-type compounds are vitamin K antagonists; K1 bypasses the block.

options.text: It destroys the platelets directly, so the blood cannot form a plug; treat with high-dose vitamin C
options.why: The mechanism is vitamin K antagonism, not platelet destruction.

options.text: It causes severe hypercalcaemia, which interferes with clotting; treat with intravenous calcium
options.why: That describes vitamin D rodenticides.

options.text: It inhibits thiamine, which clotting factors need; treat with vitamin B1 injections
options.why: Thiamine is unrelated to coagulation.

questions.stem: Cattle fed mouldy sweet clover hay develop severe internal bleeding. What is the cause?

options.text: Moulds convert coumarin in the clover to dicoumarol, a vitamin K antagonist, so factors stay inactive
options.why: This 'sweet clover disease' led to the discovery of warfarin-type anticoagulants.

options.text: Sweet clover lacks vitamin E, so the walls of blood vessels are damaged by lipid peroxidation
options.why: The problem is vitamin K antagonism.

options.text: Rumen bacteria stop producing vitamin C, so the collagen in the blood vessel walls is weakened
options.why: Cattle synthesise vitamin C in their tissues; it is unrelated to bleeding here.

options.text: Sweet clover contains excess vitamin A, which blocks the action of the clotting factors in plasma
options.why: Vitamin A excess doesn't cause this haemorrhagic syndrome.

questions.stem: Why does thiamine deficiency cause pyruvate and lactate to accumulate in the blood?

options.text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase needs TPP, so pyruvate can't become acetyl-CoA and is diverted to lactate
options.why: Blocked oxidative decarboxylation causes lactic acidosis; nervous tissue and heart are hit hardest.

options.text: Thiamine is the coenzyme for lactate dehydrogenase, so lactate cannot be converted back to pyruvate
options.why: LDH uses NADH, not TPP.

options.text: Thiamine is needed to absorb glucose, so cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis and make lactate
options.why: Glucose absorption does not depend on thiamine.

options.text: TPP is the coenzyme for transamination, so pyruvate cannot be converted into alanine
options.why: Transamination uses PLP (B6).

options.text: Pantothenic acid (B5) → coenzyme A
options.why: Its β-mercaptoethylamine –SH carries acyl groups as thioesters.

options.text: Riboflavin (B2) → NAD⁺
options.why: Riboflavin forms FMN and FAD; NAD⁺ comes from niacin.

options.text: Pyridoxine (B6) → thiamine pyrophosphate
options.why: B6 forms PLP; TPP comes from thiamine (B1).

options.text: Niacin (B3) → biotin
options.why: Biotin is B7; niacin forms NAD⁺ and NADP⁺.

questions.stem: Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) converts alanine + α-ketoglutarate into pyruvate + glutamate. Which coenzyme does it require?

options.text: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), from vitamin B6
options.why: All transaminases use PLP to carry the amino group.

options.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), from vitamin B1
options.why: TPP is for oxidative decarboxylation and transketolase.

options.text: Biotin, from vitamin B7 (vitamin H)
options.why: Biotin is for carboxylation.

options.text: Coenzyme A, from pantothenic acid (B5)
options.why: CoA carries acyl groups, not amino groups.

questions.stem: A dog fed large amounts of raw egg white develops dermatitis and hair loss. Which vitamin is affected, and why?

options.text: Biotin: avidin in raw egg white binds it so tightly that it can't be absorbed
options.why: Cooking denatures avidin; biotin is the coenzyme for carboxylases such as acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

options.text: Vitamin C: egg white contains an oxidase that destroys ascorbate in the gut
options.why: Dogs synthesise vitamin C themselves.

options.text: Vitamin K: egg-white proteins block its absorption from the small intestine
options.why: Avidin binds biotin.

options.text: Thiamine: egg white contains thiaminase, which breaks the vitamin down
options.why: Thiaminase is found in raw fish and some plants, not egg white.

questions.stem: Why can vitamin B12 deficiency cause megaloblastic anaemia even when dietary folate is adequate?

options.text: Without B12, methionine synthase can't demethylate methyl-THF, so folate is trapped and DNA synthesis slows
options.why: Thymidylate synthesis needs free THF; precursors keep growing without dividing properly.

options.text: B12 destroys dietary folate in the gut, so when B12 is missing the folate is absorbed in an inactive form
options.why: B12 doesn't destroy folate.

options.text: B12 is the iron-binding centre of haem, so without it the red cells cannot fill with functional haemoglobin
options.why: B12 contains cobalt, not iron, and is not part of haem.

options.text: B12 is required to synthesise globin chains, so the red cells grow large while waiting for globin to be made
options.why: The anaemia is due to impaired DNA synthesis, not globin synthesis.

questions.stem: Lambs grazing cobalt-deficient pasture lose weight and become anaemic, although ruminants don't need B12 in their feed. Why?

options.text: Rumen microbes make B12, which contains cobalt; without cobalt they can't make enough, so the lamb lacks B12
options.why: Ruminants also rely on B12 (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase) to use propionate for energy, so deficiency causes ill-thrift.

options.text: Cobalt is needed for haemoglobin's haem group, so without it the lamb cannot make enough red blood cells
options.why: Haem contains iron.

options.text: Cobalt is a cofactor for vitamin C synthesis in the liver, and vitamin C is needed to absorb dietary iron
options.why: Vitamin C synthesis does not depend on cobalt.

options.text: Cobalt deficiency blocks vitamin K action, so the lamb loses blood slowly through small internal bleeds
options.why: The link is cobalt → B12.

questions.stem: Most mammals can make part of their niacin requirement from tryptophan, but cats need a much higher dietary niacin intake. Why?

options.text: In cats, tryptophan breakdown diverts intermediates away from niacin, so little NAD⁺ is made
options.why: Cats rely almost entirely on dietary niacin to make NAD⁺ and NADP⁺.

options.text: Cats cannot absorb tryptophan from the gut, so little is available to be converted into niacin
options.why: Cats absorb tryptophan normally.

options.text: Niacin is a fat-soluble vitamin stored in cat liver, and cats have only a small liver store
options.why: Niacin is water-soluble.

options.text: Cats make niacin in their skin under sunlight, which indoor cats do not receive
options.why: No vitamin besides D is made in the skin.

questions.stem: Besides collagen synthesis, which role does vitamin C play in iron nutrition?

options.text: As a reducing agent it keeps dietary iron as Fe²⁺, which is absorbed more efficiently
options.why: Vitamin C also helps reduce methaemoglobin back to haemoglobin.

options.text: It forms part of the haem ring, holding the iron atom in place inside haemoglobin
options.why: Haem is a porphyrin with iron; ascorbate is not part of it.

options.text: It oxidises dietary iron to Fe³⁺ so that it can be stored safely as ferritin
options.why: Vitamin C is a reductant, not an oxidant.

options.text: It carries iron in the plasma from the gut to the bone marrow, like transferrin
options.why: Iron is carried by transferrin.

flashcards.back: Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K (need bile salts, stored, can be toxic). Water-soluble: B complex and C (mostly not stored; B12 is an exception).
Retinol (alcohol), retinal (aldehyde: vision), retinoic acid (gene expression via nuclear receptors).
Opsin + 11-cis-retinal. Light → all-trans-retinal → G-protein signal. Vitamin A deficiency → night blindness.
Acts like a steroid hormone, inducing calbindin. ↑ Gut Ca²⁺/Pi absorption, ↑ renal reabsorption, bone mineralisation, immune modulation.

flashcards.front: Vitamin E role and deficiency diseases?
flashcards.back: Membrane antioxidant (stops lipid peroxidation). Deficiency: white muscle disease (calves, lambs), mulberry heart disease (pigs), crazy chick disease.
γ-Carboxylation of Glu in factors II, VII, IX, X (and osteocalcin). Blocked by warfarin, rodenticides and dicoumarol (mouldy sweet clover). Antidote: vitamin K1.
B1 TPP · B2 FMN/FAD · B3 NAD(P)⁺ · B5 CoA · B6 PLP · B7 biotin · B9 THF · B12 cobalamin.
Transamination (ALT, AST), amino acid decarboxylation (e.g. GABA), ALA synthase (haem), glycogen phosphorylase, niacin synthesis from Trp.
Without B12, methyl-THF can't be recycled to THF, causing functional folate deficiency, megaloblastic anaemia and raised homocysteine.

flashcards.front: Which animals need dietary vitamin C? Main roles?
flashcards.back: Primates, guinea pigs and fruit bats. Roles: Pro/Lys hydroxylation (collagen), iron absorption (Fe²⁺), methaemoglobin reduction, antioxidant.
